lessons.title: How much of a notification is yours?
lessons.explanation: ATT, the Attribute Protocol, carries operations on attribute handles. An ATT maximum transmission unit (MTU) limits the entire ATT message. For a normal single-handle notification, one opcode byte and two handle bytes precede the value. The default LE ATT MTU of 23 therefore leaves up to 20 bytes for this value. Other operations have different headers.
lessons.example: A sensor wants to send 48 application bytes. At MTU 23 it takes at least three such notifications. If each part also carries a two-byte application sequence number, the usable part size becomes 18. An agreed MTU of 64 has room for all 48 bytes and the sequence number in one notification.
lessons.exercise: You negotiated MTU 64 and need to send 122 measurement bytes with a two-byte part header in every notification. How many notifications?
lessons.answer: Each carries at most 64 − 3 − 2 = 59 measurement bytes. Send three parts of 59, 59 and 4. Add a message identity if multiple messages can overlap.

lessons.title: Separate packet length from radio speed
lessons.explanation: The ATT MTU governs the upper-layer message. Data Length Extension changes how much data the link layer can carry per packet. The 2M PHY changes the symbol rate over the radio. Negotiating a larger ATT message can reduce application framing even when the controller still fragments it across several link packets. Both devices must support the selected link features.
lessons.example: Assume measured delivery of four notifications per 30 ms event, with 20 useful bytes each. Application throughput is 80 / 0.030 ≈ 2,667 bytes/s. The event interval, packets actually delivered, retransmissions and useful payload determine the observed rate. Selecting a faster PHY alone does not tell you those values.
lessons.exercise: With 100 usable bytes per delivered notification, two notifications per event, and a 50 ms interval, estimate useful throughput and the ideal transfer time for 40,000 bytes.
lessons.answer: 200 / 0.050 = 4,000 bytes/s, giving ten seconds before setup and other delays. Verify the delivered bytes over elapsed wall time on both devices.
lessons.sourceTitle: Bluetooth Core Specification · LE radio and Link Layer

lessons.title: Give every asynchronous operation a completion point
lessons.explanation: Use a per-connection queue for GATT procedures that expect a callback. Starting a characteristic read or descriptor write asks the stack to begin work; immediate acceptance does not tell you that the remote operation succeeded. Advance the queue after the matching terminal callback. Handle an immediate rejection separately because no completion may follow.
lessons.example: The queue contains discovery, a descriptor write and a read of a separate readable battery-level characteristic. Discover on this connection, select the returned handles, then write the subscription descriptor. If its callback reports failure, record that subscription failed. Issuing all operations at once makes it difficult to associate an outcome with the step that needed it.
lessons.exercise: A callback from a discarded connection arrives after a reconnect. Should it release the new connection’s next operation?
lessons.answer: No. Associate callbacks with a connection instance and current operation. End the old queue and ignore its late completion. Start the new session with fresh discovery where required.

lessons.title: Diagnose a generic GATT error
lessons.explanation: Android stacks have used decimal 133 (hexadecimal 0x85) as a generic GATT error. It identifies a failed operation without identifying a physical cause. Record the last successful transition, operation, callback, elapsed time, connection instance and permission state. A single number cannot distinguish a missing peripheral from an interrupted connection procedure.
lessons.example: Run A fails during connection, before any service discovery. Run B connects and discovers services, then fails writing a descriptor. Investigate different boundaries even if both present 133. End the failed session, release the connection resource and allow a bounded fresh attempt when the device is still wanted.
lessons.exercise: A tester wants to add an unlimited immediate retry whenever 133 appears. What evidence and policy would improve the diagnosis?
lessons.answer: Keep separate counts by stage and device pair, measure recovery for a small bounded number of delayed attempts, and stop when the user cancels or prerequisites change. Report the original stage even if a later attempt succeeds.

lessons.title: Pair once, remember deliberately
lessons.explanation: Pairing establishes security material for a connection. Bonding retains keys so the same peers can establish trusted connections later. The pairing association model depends on device capabilities and security requirements. Just Works can support encryption but supplies no user-verified authentication of the peer during pairing.
lessons.example: Two devices with suitable displays can ask their users to confirm a matching number. A screenless sensor might offer no comparable confirmation. For an application controlling access, decide how to establish that this physical sensor is the intended one and where authorization is enforced.
lessons.exercise: After the phone forgets a bond but the peripheral retains its old keys, what should a support procedure check?
lessons.answer: Check bond state on both peers and provide a deliberate reset and re-pairing path. Treat creating a new bond and granting application access as separate decisions.

lessons.title: Ask the OS for the operation you need
lessons.explanation: Android apps targeting Android 12 or later generally request nearby-device runtime permissions corresponding to discovery and communication. BLUETOOTH_SCAN covers scanning and BLUETOOTH_CONNECT covers communication with paired devices; advertising has its own permission. Older Android versions use a different permission model. Check current grants at the feature boundary.
lessons.example: A user wants to find a strap, grants scan access, then declines the permission needed to connect. The screen can explain the second operation and preserve the selected device independently of connection state. Permission denial should end that attempt without pretending the peripheral disappeared.
lessons.exercise: Your app only connects to an already known device and does not advertise. Should the onboarding flow request advertising permission?
lessons.answer: Request the operations the feature actually uses. Re-evaluate the scan and connection requirements for the supported OS and target versions, and leave advertising out of a client-only flow.

lessons.title: Make Bluetooth permission intelligible on iOS
lessons.explanation: For modern iOS apps using Bluetooth, supply the required Bluetooth purpose string in the application bundle. Explain the concrete reason for access. The displayed system authorization state, the radio’s power state and the remote device’s availability answer different questions.
lessons.example: “Connect to your heart-rate strap during a workout” describes an action the user recognizes. With access denied, show how to revisit the decision. With Bluetooth powered off, guide the user toward enabling it. Only after the app is authorized and Bluetooth is available does an empty scan describe discovery.
lessons.exercise: A screen shows “No sensors nearby” before the user has answered the permission prompt. What state should it represent instead?
lessons.answer: Represent authorization as pending and defer the empty-results message until a permitted scan has actually run. If access was denied, make that state actionable.
